cards.heading: Protecting privileged mode
cards.body: 'enable secret' stores a strong hash (type 5 MD5, or 8/9 on newer IOS). The older 'enable password' is stored in clear text (or weak type 7). If both exist, the secret is used.
cards.example:
enable secret Sup3r$ecret
!  shows as: enable secret 5 $1$mERr$hx5rVt7rPNoS4wqbXKX7m0

cards.heading: Console and VTY lines
cards.body: A line password plus 'login' asks for that password. 'login local' asks for a username and password from the local user database instead, so each admin has an account. exec-timeout logs idle sessions out.
cards.example:
line console 0
 password C0nsole!
 login
 exec-timeout 5 0
username admin secret Adm1n!Pass
line vty 0 4
 login local

cards.heading: service password-encryption
cards.body: Encrypts the clear-text passwords in the configuration (line passwords, enable password) with type 7. It only stops someone reading them over your shoulder: type 7 is easily reversed. It doesn't affect secrets, which are hashed anyway.

cards.heading: Password policy
cards.body: Good policy favours long passphrases over forced complexity, checks new passwords against known-breached lists, avoids reuse, and locks accounts after repeated failures. IOS can enforce a minimum length: 'security passwords min-length 10'.

cards.heading: Password alternatives
cards.body: Multi-factor authentication combines factors from different categories: something you know (password, PIN), something you have (phone app, token, smart card) and something you are (fingerprint, face). Digital certificates and biometrics can replace passwords altogether.
